I was washing the windows this morning. People were already talking about the accident, but I carried on with things around the house because I couldn't believe anything serious had happened. Around nine I was called urgently to the plant, and down in the bunker they explained why they needed a photographer: they need aerial photographs of the reactor to work out what's happened to it. 
 
Now I have to go up in a helicopter over Unit 4. I feel uneasy after that conversation in the bunker, although I still have no real idea what I'm going to see. When you're called in to work, you think about what needs doing, and then you find out that people are waiting for you to give them answers. 
 
I'll shoot with the Kiev-6 and take backup shots with the Zenit, so that at least one roll comes out properly. I really don't want to get back and find that you can't make anything out in the photographs.

I've come back from the flight, and they've already given me another assignment: now they need photographs from the ground. 
 
Up in the air, I had to ask them to open the window because the ash made it almost impossible to photograph anything through the glass. The military men objected, afraid of contaminating the helicopter, and I could understand them. When I leaned out with the camera, a soldier held me by the legs. I was scared, but I tried not to rush because blurred photographs wouldn't have helped anyone. 
 
I shot with both cameras, but I still don't know how the pictures have turned out. I want to get the films developed as soon as possible so I can finally see the results, but first I have to finish the second assignment. 
 
Now I'll head back to the unit with a radiation safety officer and a dosimetrist. After what I saw from above, I really don't want to go near it. I hope they'll be able to tell me where I can photograph the damage from and how close it's safe to get.

We're back from Unit 4. The road was blocked, so we had to take the fire engine along the railway, bumping over the sleepers. There was graphite lying near Unit 3; I got out to photograph it with the Zenit and left the Kiev in the cab. 
 
We got to within about fifty metres of the wreckage. While I was taking the photographs, I tried to concentrate on what needed to be in the frame, although all I wanted was to finish and leave. I took twelve pictures with each camera. We came back the same way, and what scared me most was the thought of the engine stalling, because then we'd have had to get out on foot. 
 
Now I need to develop the films. I still don't know whether anything has survived on them after that, and I can't settle down. Until I see the negatives, I'll keep thinking we might have gone there for nothing.

I developed the film from the Zenit first, and it came out black. It looks as though the radiation fogged it when I was photographing the graphite near Unit 3. My first thought was that the second roll would be the same, which would mean we'd lost everything. 
 
The images on the Kiev film survived after all, though it's gone a little cloudy. Now that I'm looking at the negatives, I can finally breathe again: these pictures will show what's happened to the reactor. While I was developing them, my biggest fear was being left with two ruined rolls and having to explain once again why there were no photographs. 
 
I need to make prints and take them to the plant. I'm glad I used both cameras, because the whole result now depends on that second set of pictures. I'm still upset about the Zenit film, but at least there's something to show the people who were waiting for us.

At the plant, the First Department took the photographs. They numbered the prints, took the films as well and told me to keep quiet about everything I'd seen and heard. 
 
While I was taking the photographs, all I could think about was getting those pictures back to them. Then I was afraid nothing would come out when I developed the film, and now I don't even know whether I'll ever see my photographs again. I understand why the management needs them, but it's still hard to hand over the film when I remember what it took to get every frame. 
 
I don't know whether they'll show them to anyone, or who'll even be allowed to look. After being told to keep quiet, I don't much feel like asking, although I've only got more questions now. 
 
Now I need to get home. They'll want to know what's happening at the plant too, and I still have no idea how to explain where I've spent the day or why there's so little I can tell them.

I got home around midnight and started throwing up. My face is red, my throat is burning and there's a sore on my forehead. At work there was always something urgent left to do, and I thought I'd finally be able to rest once I got home. Now I can't just lie down and put the day behind me. 
 
My wife is here, trying to help, and I don't know what to tell her. I want to reassure her, to say that all I need is a good night's sleep, but I'm not sure I'll feel any better by morning. After where we've been today, putting it all down to exhaustion would be too convenient. 
 
I'll try to rest for now. I want to wake up in the morning and feel better, because right now I can't even reassure my wife properly.

I'm in Moscow now, in Hospital No. 6. I got so ill in the autumn that an ambulance had to take me away from work. Until then I'd kept taking photographs: we needed to show how the sarcophagus was being built. I photographed the unit from the ground and flew over it in a military helicopter twice a week. 
 
The pictures let people follow the construction, and I understood why each new trip was needed. Whenever I finished the job, I wanted to believe I could manage whatever came next. Back in April, I thought all I needed was a bit of rest, too. 
 
Right now I want to understand what's wrong with me and when I'll be able to get back to work, but I don't have that confidence any more. I keep thinking about that first day, although there's nothing I can change about it now. I need treatment, yet I still catch myself trying to work out how many shoots I'll miss.

Anatoly gave me these notes when I told him I was planning to go to Pripyat. We've known each other for years, but all I knew about those photographs was what he occasionally told me. I promised I'd try to retrace his route and bring back photographs. I'll take these pages with me so I can refer to them along the way, and I'll start in town — I still need to find a way to reach the plant.%c[default]

They've returned a few of the photographs I took on the day of the accident. It's been nearly twenty years since that shoot, but I still remember the soldier holding me by the legs, and how afraid we were afterwards that the engine would stall near the unit. 
 
Two of the pictures were printed back in 1987, in "Chernobyl Report", but my name wasn't there. It's an unpleasant feeling, looking at a photograph I know so well and seeing no mention of me beneath it. I can tell you which camera I used and how worried I was about the film when I got back. 
 
Now I want to sort through what they've given me and label every photograph: when it was taken, where I was standing, who was with me. I need to write those things down while I still remember them. I really don't want the photographs to end up in other people's hands again, with everything behind them needing to be explained all over again. 
 
%c[255,238,153,26]A note is written below 
 
I never made it to the plant. After the fall, all I could do was crawl to shelter and bandage my leg, but the bandage is already soaked through, and whenever I try to stand up, my vision goes dark. 
 
I promised Anatoly I'd bring back photographs, and now I don't know whether I'll even make it out. I'll leave the camera and these notes here, because I can't carry them any farther. First I need to stop the bleeding, and then I'll try…%c[default]
